t: The Hoabinhian is a tradition of stone tools, chiefly flaked river cobbles, left by hunter-gatherers across mainland Southeast Asia from the late Pleistocene to the Holocene.

It was first defined from Madeleine Colani’s excavations in Hòa Bình province, northern Vietnam, but later study showed that its tools form a continuous range of shapes and sizes rather than distinct types.
Ancient DNA from two Hoabinhian individuals shows a deeply branching East Asian ancestry, shared most closely today with peoples such as the Andamanese Onge and Jarawa, the Semang and the Maniq.
dyk: Madeleine Colani sorted just 82 artefacts from Sao Dong into 28 types; her typology proved so complicated that most Hoabinhian sites are identified simply by the presence of sumatraliths.
ev: The Bacsonian variant, richer in edge-ground cobble tools, is made in northern Vietnam
Cord-marked pottery appears in the Hoabinhian levels of Spirit Cave in northwest Thailand
Madeleine Colani publishes her nine excavations in the northern Vietnamese province of Hòa Bình
The First Congress of Prehistorians of the Far East defines the Hoabinhian
J. M. Matthews shows that the cobble tools of Sai Yok form a continuous range rather than Colani’s distinct types
A conference in Hanoi votes to keep the term and to call the Hoabinhian an industry of the late Pleistocene to mid Holocene
Hoabinhian artefacts dating from 41,500 BCE are recognised at the Xiaodong rock shelter in Yunnan, 40 km from the border with Myanmar

f.homeland: Mainland Southeast Asia: more than 120 sites in Vietnam, among them those of Hòa Bình province and Da But; Spirit Cave, Sai Yok, Tham Lod and Ban Rai in Thailand; Pha Faen in Laos; Gua Cha in Malaysia; sites in Terengganu, Sumatra, Laos, Myanmar and Cambodia; and Xiaodong in Yunnan, China, the oldest and the only one in China.
f.period: Usually dated c. 10,000–2000 BCE, from the late Pleistocene to the Holocene; the 1994 Hanoi conference set it at the “late-to-terminal Pleistocene to early-to-mid Holocene”. Xiaodong dates from 41,500 BCE, Vietnamese finds to 17,000 years before the present, Spirit Cave’s Hoabinhian levels to 12,000–8000 BP; the Bacsonian variant c. 8000–4000 BCE.
f.known: flaked cobble tools, often worked on one face only; sumatraliths, cobbles flaked all over one side; grinding stones, often found with iron oxide; rock shelters near streams in limestone uplands; shell middens; edge-ground tools and cord-marked pottery in the upper layers; plant remains at Spirit Cave
f.sources: Madeleine Colani’s excavations in Hòa Bình province, published in 1927, and the 1932 definition of the First Congress of Prehistorians of the Far East; J. M. Matthews’s 1964 study at Sai Yok; Chester Gorman’s excavations and radiocarbon dates at Spirit Cave; the 1994 Hanoi conference; ancient DNA from Pha Faen and Gua Cha.
